The philosopher's treatment of temporal awareness reveals itself as fundamentally grounded in the dynamic relationship between motion and consciousness, where time appears not as an abstract container but as the measure of change that becomes accessible through the complex interplay of perception, imagination, and intellective activity. Indeed, Aristotle's  temporal consciousness requires both the immediate responsiveness of sensation and the synthetic capacity of higher cognitive faculties, particularly phantasia, which serves as the crucial mediating function between sensory experience and conceptual understanding. Hence, we must examine how Aristotelian temporality unfolds through the intricate coordination of kinesis, aisthēsis, and phantasia as they constitute the fundamental structures of temporal awareness. ## Aristotle on Motion

Motion (kinesis) occupies a foundational position within Aristotelian philosophy precisely because it provides the ontological ground from which temporal experience emerges; accordingly, Heidegger observes that "kinesis gives the authentic Da-Charakter to Dasein, the vital place-time of Being" (*Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). The significance of this observation lies in its recognition that motion is not merely a physical phenomenon but constitutes the basic character of existence itself, the fundamental way in which beings maintain their dynamic engagement with the world around them. Aristotle's definition of motion reveals its essential structure: it represents the actualization of potential insofar as it remains potential, a formulation that captures the peculiar ontological status of change as neither pure potentiality nor complete actuality but rather the active process of becoming that bridges these metaphysical categories. Thus, motion emerges as "a how of the being of beings that are there determined in the form of being of the categories" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 262), indicating that kinesis provides the fundamental mode through which beings manifest their essential character within the categorical structure of reality. The philosophical importance of motion extends beyond its role as a physical process to encompass its function as the condition that makes temporal awareness possible; specifically, motion provides the underlying rhythm and measure through which consciousness apprehends the passage of time and the sequential ordering of experience. Motion reveals itself as inherently relational, always involving the movement from one state to another, the transition between determinate positions that creates the spatial and temporal intervals within which conscious experience unfolds. Similarly, motion exhibits a complex internal structure that encompasses not only the moving entity but also the spatial field through which movement occurs and the temporal duration that movement requires, thereby establishing motion as a fundamentally synthetic phenomenon that unifies space, time, and being within a single dynamic process. ## Aristotle on Time

Time emerges within Aristotelian analysis as intimately connected to motion while maintaining its own distinctive character as the measure of change; hence, Aristotle's investigation reveals time as "the number of motion in respect of the before and after," a formulation that establishes time's dependence upon motion while emphasizing its role as the quantitative dimension through which change becomes intelligible. The philosophical sophistication of this account lies in its recognition that time requires both the objective occurrence of motion and the subjective capacity to apprehend and measure that motion, thus revealing temporal experience as necessarily involving both ontological and epistemological dimensions. Indeed, the Aristotelian  time possesses a peculiar ontological status that is neither purely objective nor purely subjective but rather emerges from the dynamic interaction between changing beings and the consciousness that apprehends those changes. Bowin observes that "measuring time by counting determinate units of time like days, we apprehend (γνωρίζειν) time and the amount of time determinately" (*Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, p. 8), indicating that temporal cognition requires the intellectual capacity to grasp universal concepts and apply them to the measurement of duration. The complexity of Aristotelian temporality becomes evident in its distinction between the perception of time and the cognition of time, where perception provides the immediate awareness of temporal succession while cognition enables the precise measurement and conceptual understanding of temporal intervals. Thus, temporal experience exhibits a hierarchical structure that encompasses the basic perceptual recognition of before and after, the imaginative synthesis of temporal sequences, and the intellectual comprehension of temporal measurement, each level building upon and presupposing the capacities that precede it. The philosophical significance of this analysis extends to its implications for understanding human existence as fundamentally temporal, where the capacity for temporal awareness emerges as a defining characteristic that distinguishes conscious beings from entities that merely undergo change without apprehending their own temporal situation. ## The Relation Between Motion and Time

The intricate relationship between motion and time within Aristotelian philosophy reveals itself through their mutual dependence and reciprocal determination, where motion provides the ontological foundation for temporal experience while time serves as the measure through which motion becomes intelligible and determinate. This reciprocity indicates that neither motion nor time can be adequately understood in isolation from the other; rather, they form a unified ontological structure that constitutes the fundamental framework within which all change and development occur. Accordingly, Heidegger emphasizes that "the ontological significance of the passions lies in our capacity for change, the Veränderlichkeit of Being" (*Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115), suggesting that the relationship between motion and time extends beyond mere physical processes to encompass the emotional and dispositional dimensions of existence that enable beings to be affected by and responsive to their temporal situation. The philosophical depth of this relationship emerges in its recognition that motion and time together constitute the basic structure of becoming, the fundamental process through which beings actualize their potentialities and unfold their essential nature across temporal duration. Thus, the Aristotelian analysis reveals that temporal consciousness necessarily involves the capacity to apprehend not only discrete moments but also the dynamic transitions between moments, the continuous flow of change that creates the temporal field within which conscious experience occurs. Similarly, this  conscious beings do not merely exist within time but rather participate actively in the creation of temporality through their capacity to perceive, remember, and anticipate the sequential unfolding of their experience. The significance of this participation lies in its indication that temporal consciousness involves a complex synthesis of past, present, and future that enables beings to orient themselves within the ongoing flow of temporal experience and to act purposefully within that temporal context. ## Aisthēsis and Temporal Awareness

Sensory perception (aisthēsis) provides the foundational level of temporal awareness through its capacity to register the immediate presence of changing phenomena and to discriminate between successive perceptual states; hence, aisthetic consciousness supplies the basic temporal content that higher cognitive faculties subsequently organize and interpret within more complex temporal structures. The philosophical importance of aisthēsis lies in its function as the primary interface between conscious beings and the temporal world, the capacity through which the ongoing flow of environmental change becomes accessible to consciousness as a series of discriminable perceptual moments. Indeed, Aristotelian analysis reveals that sensory perception inherently involves temporal synthesis, since every perceptual act encompasses not only the immediate apprehension of present stimuli but also the retention of immediately past perceptual states and the anticipation of immediately forthcoming perceptual changes. Bowin notes that "apprehending time indeterminately, on the other hand, seems only to be an achievement of perception" (*Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, p. 8), indicating that perception provides a direct but non-conceptual awareness of temporal passage that serves as the foundation for more sophisticated forms of temporal cognition. The complexity of aisthetic temporal awareness becomes evident in its capacity to apprehend not merely isolated sensory qualities but also the dynamic patterns and rhythms that emerge across sequences of perceptual experience; thus, perception enables consciousness to recognize the temporal structure of environmental change and to anticipate future developments based upon the discernment of ongoing perceptual patterns. This anticipatory dimension of aisthēsis reveals its essential connection to the temporal structure of conscious engagement with the world, where perceptual awareness necessarily involves the projection of consciousness beyond the immediate present toward the temporal horizons that bound and orient current experience. Similarly, the temporal character of perception indicates that aisthetic consciousness participates actively in the constitution of temporal experience rather than merely receiving temporal content from external sources, thereby revealing perception as a fundamentally creative and synthetic activity that contributes to the ongoing formation of temporal awareness. ## Phantasia and Temporal Unification

The imagination (phantasia) emerges within Aristotelian psychology as the crucial faculty that enables the synthetic unification of temporal experience through its capacity to preserve, combine, and project the images that derive from sensory perception; accordingly, phantasia serves as the essential mediating function between the immediate temporality of aisthēsis and the conceptual temporality of intellectual cognition. 4), indicating that imaginative consciousness occupies a pivotal position within the hierarchical structure of temporal awareness, where it receives and synthesizes the temporal content provided by perception while making that content available for further intellectual processing. The philosophical significance of phantasia lies in its capacity to transcend the limitations of immediate sensory experience by creating complex temporal syntheses that encompass extended temporal sequences and enable consciousness to apprehend temporal wholes that exceed the scope of any single perceptual moment. The temporal function of phantasia reveals itself most clearly in its role as the faculty that enables memory, anticipation, and temporal deliberation through its capacity to make absent temporal contents present to consciousness in the form of mental images that preserve and represent past experiences while projecting possible future developments. Thus, imaginative consciousness enables beings to inhabit a temporal world that extends far beyond the immediate present, creating the expanded temporal horizon within which purposeful action and meaningful choice become possible. Indeed, the Aristotelian  phantasia provides the essential foundation for the temporal dimensions of practical wisdom, enabling conscious beings to deliberate about future action by imaginatively projecting the consequences of different possible courses of action and by drawing upon the accumulated wisdom preserved in memory through imaginative representation. 4), emphasizing the comprehensive scope of imaginative temporal synthesis and its fundamental importance for the full range of conscious temporal engagement with the world. ## Heidegger's Interpretation of Aristotle

Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotelian temporality reveals its profound significance for understanding the existential structure of Dasein and the fundamental constitution of temporal being-in-the-world; thus, Heidegger discovers within Aristotelian analysis resources for articulating a more originary understanding of temporality that overcomes the traditional metaphysical conception of time as a series of discrete moments. The philosophical depth of Heidegger's reading lies in its recognition that Aristotelian concepts of motion, time, and consciousness point toward a more fundamental temporal structure that encompasses not merely the objective measurement of temporal intervals but the existential temporality that constitutes the basic character of human existence. Hence, Heidegger observes that Aristotelian psychology reveals "being-in-a-world" as the fundamental structure of living beings (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 177), indicating that temporal consciousness cannot be separated from the broader existential structure that constitutes conscious beings as essentially worldly and essentially temporal. The significance of Heidegger's interpretation extends to its demonstration that Aristotelian analysis of the passions (pathē) reveals the dispositional character of temporal consciousness, where emotional responsiveness and temporal awareness emerge as fundamentally interconnected dimensions of existential being-in-the-world. Accordingly, Heidegger emphasizes that "passions are dispositions oriented on others' dispositions that define our in-the-worldness" (*Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115), revealing that temporal consciousness necessarily involves attunement to the temporal rhythms and patterns that characterize both individual existence and communal life. This dispositional understanding of temporality indicates that temporal awareness emerges not through detached observation but through engaged participation in the temporal structures that constitute the shared world within which conscious beings encounter one another and coordinate their activities. Similarly, Heidegger's reading reveals that Aristotelian temporality points toward a conception of dwelling that encompasses both the temporal and spatial dimensions of existential inhabitation, where conscious beings create and maintain temporal places through their ongoing engagement with the environmental and social contexts that surround and sustain their existence. ---
